accepted.question_text: Let K_0, K_1, K_2, K_3, S, M, and G be the classes of groups considered in the paper, and recall that Theorem 1.1 proves the following statement whenever A and B are members of this collection with B properly contained in A and A containing K_3: there is no algorithm that decides, given a finite presentation of a group known to lie in A, whether that group lies in B. Does the same undecidability statement remain true in the case A = K_2?

evidence.quote: Theorem 1.1. Let A and B be members of {K0, K1, K2, K3, S,M, G} such that B ( A and A ⊃ K3. Then there does not exist an algorithm that can decide, given a finite presentation of a group G in A whether or not G is in B.
We conjecture that Theorem 1.1 also holds for A = K2; we show that this is true if there is a group in K2 with unsolvable word problem.

accepted.question_text: Is the isomorphism problem for 2-knot groups algorithmically unsolvable? In other words, is there no algorithm that takes finite presentations of two groups known to belong to K_2, the class of groups of 2-knots, and always decides whether the two groups are isomorphic?

evidence.quote: The case A = K3 and B = K0 of Theorem 1.1 implies that the isomorphism problem for K3 and the other three classes containing it is unsolvable. Conjecturally this should hold also for K2.
For n ≥ 0 we define Kn to be the class of groups of n-knots.

accepted.question_text: Does there exist a 2-knot group with unsolvable word problem? Here K_2 is the class of groups of 2-knots, so the question asks whether some group of a 2-knot has no algorithm deciding, for an arbitrary word in its generators, whether that word represents the identity element.

evidence.quote: Though we do not know whether 2-knot groups with unsolvable word problem exist, we prove (Corollary 3.5) that there are 3-knot groups with unsolvable word problem.
For n ≥ 0 we define Kn to be the class of groups of n-knots.
(1) Is there a 2-knot group with unsolvable word problem? Conjecture: Yes.

accepted.question_text: Does every finitely presented group embed in a 2-knot group? That is, for each finitely presented group G, must there exist a group in K_2, the class of groups of 2-knots, that contains an isomorphic copy of G as a subgroup?

evidence.quote: (2) Does each finitely presented group embed in a 2-knot group? Conjecture: Yes.
For n ≥ 0 we define Kn to be the class of groups of n-knots.

accepted.question_text: In the setting of Theorem 5.1, let C be a class of infinite sequences of abelian groups, closed under isomorphism, such that there exist finitely presented groups G_1 and G_2 with the same first homology H_1(G_1) isomorphic to H_1(G_2), with H_*(G_1) in C and H_*(G_2) not in C. Theorem 5.1 proves that the set of finite presentations P for which the integral homology sequence H_*(P) belongs to C is not recursive. Under what additional hypotheses on C can this conclusion be strengthened by replacing 'not recursive' with 'not recursively enumerable'?

evidence.quote: Theorem 5.1. Let C be a class of infinite sequences (A1, A2, A3, . . .) of abelian groups which is closed under isomorphisms. Suppose there are finitely presented groups G1, G2 such that H1(G1) ∼= H1(G2), H∗(G1) ∈ C and H∗(G2) ∈ C /. Then the set of finite presentations P such that H∗(P) ∈ C is not recursive.
Question 5.2. When can one replace recursive by recursively enumerable?
